title: Mencius
author: mencius
attributionNote: The book is named for Mencius (Meng Ke, c. 371–289 BCE) and was compiled by him and his disciples; the seven books record his arguments with rulers and rival teachers, and their editorship is debated.
description: Mencius is the second book of the Four Books: seven books of argument and anecdote in which Meng Ke tells King Hui of Liang what a benevolent government would be, contends that human nature is good and that compassion is its seed, distinguishes the great man from the petty, defends Confucius against the Mohists and the agriculturalists, and sets out the people's right to judge a ruler who has lost heaven's mandate.
historicalContext: The book circulated as a separate classic and was elevated into the Four Books by Zhu Xi, who read its teaching of the goodness of human nature as the foundation of Neo-Confucian ethics. James Legge published his translation, with the Chinese text and extensive notes, as the second volume of The Chinese Classics (1895).
availabilityNote: Complete in Legge's translation: all seven books as the archive prints them in twenty-eight chapters, streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time. Legge's prolegomena, his exegetical notes and the Chinese text are volume apparatus and are not part of the work.
